 Social Security Spousal Benefits Are Getting Their Biggest Boost in 4 Years: What Married Retirees Need to Know
 Maurie Backman Updated 2026년 11월 8일 일 오후 11:00 UTC 0 oneinchpunch / Shutterstock.com (oneinchpunch / Shutterstock.com) Quick Read
 Social Security spousal benefits max out at 50% of a qualifying spouse's full retirement age benefit and cannot grow with delayed claiming.
 A projected 2027 COLA somewhere between 3.4% and 3.6% could push the average spousal benefit above $1,000, up from roughly $987 today.
 Working in retirement can help spousal benefit recipients qualify for their own Social Security, potentially earning higher monthly payments.
 Are you ahead, or behind on retirement? SmartAsset's free tool can match you with a financial advisor in minutes to help you answer that today. Each advisor has been carefully vetted, and must act in your best interests. Don't waste another minute; learn more here. 
 Most people earn Social Security by working and paying taxes on their wages throughout their careers. Anyone who accumulates 40 work credits over a lifetime qualifies for retirement benefits, with up to four credits available per calendar year. The dollar value of a single credit adjusts annually, so the threshold rises modestly with wage growth over time.
 For those who do not qualify for Social Security on their own earnings record, spousal benefits offer a meaningful alternative. Anyone married to a Social Security-eligible retiree can claim on that spouse's record. Eligible divorced spouses can access the same benefit, provided the marriage lasted at least ten years.
 The structural limitation of spousal benefits is straightforward: they cap at 50% of the qualifying spouse's full retirement age (FRA) benefit. Someone whose spouse qualifies for a $2,000 monthly benefit at FRA would receive a maximum spousal benefit of $1,000. Claiming before your own FRA reduces that amount. And unlike benefits earned on your own record, spousal benefits earn no delayed retirement credits past FRA. Workers who defer their own benefit past FRA receive an 8% annual boost up to age 70. Spousal claimants get no such reward for waiting beyond their own FRA.
 The good news is that Social Security spousal benefits are now confirmed to receive a meaningful increase in 2027. Here is what happened.

 A confirmed 3.6% COLA pushes the average spousal check past $1,000
 Social Security benefits are adjusted for inflation each year through a cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. The SSA calculates the COLA by comparing the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) during the third quarter of the current year against the same quarter one year prior. On October 14, 2026, the SSA officially announced the 2027 COLA at 3.6%, the largest increase in four years and well above the 20-year historical average of 2.6%.
 Heading into that announcement, independent forecasters had converged on a range of 3.5% to 3.6%. Both The Senior Citizens League, a nonpartisan senior advocacy group, and AARP projected a 3.5% COLA for 2027 based on data available before the final September inflation figures were released. The confirmed 3.6% came in at the top of that range, comfortably above the 2.8% adjustment that took effect in January 2026 and the 2.5% increase that preceded it.
 Advertisement
 The average Social Security spousal benefit stood at approximately $986 per month as of September 2026. The confirmed 3.6% COLA adds roughly $35 to that figure, bringing the projected average to approximately $1,021 per month in January 2027. That would mark the first time the typical spousal benefit has crossed the $1,000 threshold, a milestone that carries real practical weight for retirees on fixed incomes. Spousal beneficiaries can expect a personalized notice from the SSA in December showing their exact new monthly amount.
 Why spousal benefits alone are rarely enough
 Spousal benefits are essential for people without a strong earnings history, but they are modest by design. The average spousal benefit of roughly $986 per month is the highest it has ever been, yet it still amounts to less than half of the average retirement benefit of $2,095 for all retired workers in 2026. Building additional income streams through savings, investment accounts, or part-time work remains critical for most retirees who rely primarily on spousal payments.
 Working in retirement creates a specific opportunity for spousal benefit recipients. Every year of additional covered earnings can update the wage history underlying a potential benefit on your own record. If that personal benefit eventually exceeds the spousal benefit, Social Security pays the higher amount automatically. Someone with a $1,100 monthly benefit based on their own record would receive that amount rather than a $1,000 spousal benefit. The reverse holds as well: if the personal record yields a smaller figure, the spousal benefit applies. This dynamic gives part-time work in retirement a compounding advantage beyond the paycheck itself, since additional covered earnings could translate into a permanently larger Social Security check.
 Editor's note: This article was updated to reflect the SSA's official 2027 COLA announcement of 3.6% on October 14, 2026, the highest adjustment in four years, along with the confirmed September 2026 average spousal benefit of $986 per month and the resulting projected 2027 average of approximately $1,021 per month.
